title: Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease
blurb: Recognise bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease in children using NICE NG240, act on a non-blanching rash, and know the rules on transfer, antibiotics, steroids and follow-up.
question: Ellie, 6, has a fever, a spreading purpuric rash and cold hands. The GP strongly suspects meningococcal disease and has called an ambulance, which will arrive in 10 minutes. What should happen about antibiotics?

teach.body: Bacterial meningitis is infection and inflammation of the meninges around the brain and spinal cord. Meningococcal disease is infection with Neisseria meningitidis, which can cause meningitis, septicaemia or both. Both evolve rapidly and can start with non-specific signs, especially in young babies. NICE NG240 (March 2024) is the current guideline; it replaced CG102. Plain English: a feverish child who is getting worse fast, especially with a rash that does not fade, needs hospital now.
teach.cite: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (Mar 2024)

rows.label: Strongly suspect if
values: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered consciousness together
Purpura over 2 mm, or spreading non-blanching rash

rows.label: Also
values: Can be strongly suspected without all four
Meningitis signs plus a non-blanching rash

rows.label: In babies
values: Bulging fontanelle; fever and neck stiffness less common
Rash may be absent: do not rule it out

teach.caption: Meningitis and sepsis can occur together, particularly in a child with a rash.

items: Check all over the body, including nappy areas.
Look for petechiae in the conjunctivae, especially on brown, black or tanned skin.
Tell families a rash can change from blanching to non-blanching.
Do not rule out meningococcal disease because there is no rash.
Ask whether antipyretics were given: they can make a fever harder to identify.

steps.label: Emergency transfer
steps.sub: Tell the hospital: senior decision maker needed

steps.label: Meningococcal strongly suspected
steps.sub: IV or IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin as soon as possible

steps.label: Strongly suspected meningitis
steps.sub: Give pre-hospital antibiotic if transfer delay is clinically significant

teach.caption: Do not give pre-hospital antibiotics if there is severe allergy to ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin.

head: Step
Detail
rows: IV within 1 hour of arrival with suspected bacterial meningitis
Bloods; LP only if safe and no significant delay
IV for over 3 months with bacterial meningitis
teach.caption: Continue dexamethasone if the organism is pneumococcus or Hib; stop it for other organisms.

teach.text: Do not keep the child waiting for a lumbar puncture or for antibiotics in the community. NG240 says LP before antibiotics only if it is safe and causes no clinically significant delay, and transfer must not be delayed to give pre-hospital antibiotics.

teach.h: Scenario: Sami, 18 months, at the practice
teach.body: Sami has a fever and is irritable. His skin is dark brown and nurse Kerry cannot see a rash on his trunk. She checks his conjunctivae and finds petechiae, and also checks his nappy area. Recognising a possible non-blanching rash with fever, she arranges emergency transfer by 999 and alerts the GP, who gives IM ceftriaxone without delaying the ambulance.

items.label: audiology within 4 weeks of being well enough
cochlear implant assessment if severe deafness
ceftriaxone for meningococcal disease, then review

teach.caption: Plan follow-up for complications such as hearing loss, skin and limb damage, and psychological effects.

items: Strongly suspect meningococcal disease with purpura over 2 mm, a spreading non-blanching rash, or meningitis signs plus a non-blanching rash.
Look for petechiae in the conjunctivae and nappy area; no rash does not exclude it.
Emergency transfer; pre-hospital IV or IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin without delaying transfer.
Hospital: IV antibiotics within 1 hour; LP first only if safe and quick; dexamethasone for over 3 months.
Audiology within 4 weeks of being well enough.

summary: You can now recognise bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease using NG240 red flags, examine for rashes properly on all skin tones and act without delay. You can also explain the hospital steps, the role of dexamethasone and the need for hearing follow-up.

A.q: Ellie, 6, has fever, a spreading purpuric rash and cold hands. The GP strongly suspects meningococcal disease. An ambulance will arrive in 10 minutes. What should happen about antibiotics?
options: Wait for hospital blood cultures first
Give IM or IV ceftriaxone now
Delay transfer until antibiotics are given
A.why: NG240 rec 1.2.5: with strongly suspected meningococcal disease, give IV or IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin as soon as possible outside hospital, unless it delays transfer.

whyNot.0: Waiting for cultures in hospital delays treatment of a rapidly fatal illness.
whyNot.1: Oral antibiotics are not the recommended pre-hospital treatment.
whyNot.3: NG240 says do not delay transfer to give antibiotics.

A.q: Lily, 3, has a fever and is now drowsy. Her father noticed a few dark red spots on her legs that do not fade with pressure. What should the nurse do?
options: Give paracetamol and review her in 1 hour
Book a GP review for later today
Mark the spots and review tomorrow
A.why: Fever, drowsiness and a non-blanching rash suggest meningococcal disease: transfer to hospital as an emergency.

whyNot.1: Antipyretics can mask illness, and waiting an hour is unsafe.
whyNot.2: A later appointment delays emergency care.
whyNot.3: Rashes can spread rapidly; waiting until tomorrow could be fatal.

A.q: Sami, 18 months, has a fever and is irritable. His skin is dark brown and no rash is seen on his trunk. Where should the nurse also look for petechiae?
A.why: NG240: rashes can be hard to see on brown, black or tanned skin; look for petechiae in the conjunctivae and check all over, including nappy areas.

whyNot.0: The scalp is part of the all-over check but NG240 highlights the conjunctivae.
whyNot.2: The tongue is not the site named for petechiae in NG240.
whyNot.3: Nail beds are not the site NG240 recommends for petechiae.

B.q: Ishaan, 4, is admitted with suspected bacterial meningitis. How soon should IV antibiotics start?
options: After the LP result is known
B.why: NG240 rec 1.4.1: antibiotics start within 1 hour of arrival at hospital with suspected bacterial meningitis.

whyNot.0: 3 hours is too long for suspected bacterial meningitis.
whyNot.1: 4 hours is far outside the NG240 standard.
whyNot.2: Waiting for LP results would delay antibiotics.

B.q: Freya, 2, has confirmed bacterial meningitis and was started on IV dexamethasone. Cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae. What should happen to the dexamethasone?
options: Stop it once cultures are back
Stop it once she is afebrile
B.why: NG240 rec 1.8.3: continue dexamethasone if the organism is pneumococcus or Hib; stop it for other organisms.

whyNot.0: It is stopped for other organisms, not pneumococcus.
whyNot.1: Fever settling is not the rule for stopping it.
whyNot.2: NG240 continues IV dexamethasone; it does not switch to prednisolone.

B.q: Noor, 9 months, has a fever. A single small spot on her chest blanched when checked an hour ago. What advice should the nurse give her parents?
options: The rash can change to non-blanching
Spots on the chest are harmless
B.why: NG240 rec 1.1.12: tell families to watch for changes because a rash can change from blanching to non-blanching.

whyNot.1: A blanching rash does not exclude meningitis or meningococcal disease.
whyNot.2: Waiting until tomorrow is too long for a febrile infant.
whyNot.3: The site of a rash does not make it harmless.

C.q: Jamal, 7, is recovering from pneumococcal meningitis and is due home next week. His mother asks what follow-up he needs. Which is essential?
options: A brain MRI scan at 6 months
C.why: NG240 rec 1.12.7: offer audiological assessment within 4 weeks of being well enough, preferably before discharge.

whyNot.0: A repeat LP is not routine follow-up.
whyNot.1: Blood cultures are not repeated routinely after recovery.
whyNot.2: Routine MRI is not part of NG240 follow-up.

C.q: Mia, 14 months, has fever and irritability. Her rash blanches, but she has a bulging fontanelle and a weak high-pitched cry. What is the most appropriate action?
C.why: A bulging fontanelle suggests bacterial meningitis (NG240 table 1) and a weak high-pitched cry is red in NG143. Emergency transfer is needed.

whyNot.0: A blanching rash does not exclude meningitis.
whyNot.1: Delaying 4 hours is unsafe with these features.
whyNot.3: Safety-netting is for low risk; these are high risk signs.

C.q: A 15-year-old with suspected bacterial meningitis is in the emergency department. The LP will take 2 hours to arrange. What should happen?
options: Wait for the LP, then give antibiotics
Take bloods and give antibiotics now
Give dexamethasone alone until the LP
C.why: NG240: take blood samples, and only do the LP before antibiotics if it causes no clinically significant delay. Antibiotics must start within 1 hour.

whyNot.0: A 2-hour wait would breach the 1-hour antibiotic standard.
whyNot.3: Dexamethasone does not replace antibiotics, and should not delay them.

reteach.title: Fast illness, fast action
reteach.question: Why does NG240 keep saying 'do not delay'?

blocks.body: Meningococcal disease can progress from a well-looking child to shock within hours. So the rules all aim at speed: transfer as an emergency, give antibiotics before arrival if meningococcal disease is strongly suspected (without holding up the ambulance), and start IV antibiotics within 1 hour of arrival. Tests that would slow this down are skipped or done later.

items.label: IV antibiotics (LP first only if quick)

blocks.text: Pressing on a rash is only one check. A blanching rash today can become non-blanching later, and some children have no rash at all.

explain.body: Bacterial meningitis red flag combination: fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered consciousness. Babies may show a bulging fontanelle; fever and neck stiffness are less common in babies.

test.q: Which sign in an infant is listed in NG240 as suggesting bacterial meningitis?
test.why: A bulging fontanelle is listed for babies and young children with an open fontanelle.

whyNot.2: Nasal flaring is a respiratory sign.
whyNot.3: Strawberry tongue is linked with Kawasaki disease.

explain.body: Strongly suspect meningococcal disease with purpura over 2 mm, a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash, or meningitis signs plus a non-blanching rash. Check all over and the conjunctivae.

test.q: What size of haemorrhagic non-blanching lesion is a red flag for meningococcal disease?
test.why: NG240 rec 1.1.9: a haemorrhagic non-blanching rash with lesions larger than 2 mm (purpura).

whyNot.1: 5 mm is larger than the stated threshold.
whyNot.3: 10 mm is far larger than the threshold.

explain.body: Transfer as an emergency. Meningococcal disease strongly suspected: IV or IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin as soon as possible, unless it would delay transfer. Not if severe allergy to either.

test.q: Which antibiotics does NG240 list for use before hospital?
test.why: NG240 rec 1.2.4–1.2.5: IV or IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin.

whyNot.1: These are oral agents not named in NG240 for this.
whyNot.2: These are not the recommended pre-hospital antibiotics.
whyNot.3: These are not named in NG240 for pre-hospital treatment.

explain.body: IV antibiotics within 1 hour; LP first only if safe and quick. IV dexamethasone for over 3 months with bacterial meningitis; continue only for pneumococcus or Hib. Audiology within 4 weeks of being well enough.

test.q: In which age group does NG240 recommend IV dexamethasone for strongly suspected bacterial meningitis?
test.why: NG240 rec 1.8.1: give IV dexamethasone to people over 3 months with strongly suspected or confirmed bacterial meningitis.

whyNot.1: 28 days to 3 months needs infection specialist advice.
whyNot.3: It is not routine under 3 months: newborns follow neonatal guidance and 28 days to 3 months needs infection specialist advice.
